L8@P0: Abstract
L9@P0: Cryptoasset systems often bind cryptographic key control to financial control: losing a wallet
L10@P0: seed, custody share, hardware device, or smart-account credential can remove spend authority,
L11@P0: while compromised recovery can enable theft. Existing work treats recovery through separate
L12@P0: vocabularies–key backup, secret sharing, account recovery, credential re-issuance, social recovery,
L13@P0: and asset migration–making mechanisms and tradeoffs difficult to compare.
L14@P0: This paper presents a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on cryptographic key recovery for
L15@P0: cryptoasset custody and financial technologies. Starting from a 118-paper systematic-review discovery
L16@P0: corpus, we derive a 77-paper synthesis corpus and code each retained system in a master matrix
L17@P0: covering recovered objects, recovery semantics, mechanisms, enrollment and storage, authorization,
L18@P0: trust placement, failure events, post-recovery state, validation evidence, deployment status, privacy,
L19@P0: usability, and limitations. The matrix supports an axis-first taxonomy that separates secret-restoring,
L20@P0: hybrid, control-restoring, forensic/extractive, and framework-oriented recovery.
L21@P0: Our central observation is that recovery is not a single operation: systems may reconstruct an
L22@P0: original secret, regenerate a seed, restore a share, reissue a credential, migrate signing authority,
L23@P0: restore account control, move assets, or extract forensic artifacts. We derive a generalized construction
L24@P0: model, check it against production-facing designs, and identify six findings: recovery semantics are
L25@P0: heterogeneous; recovery shifts trust; liveness improvements create abuse paths; post-recovery lifecycle
L26@P0: management is uneven; protocol evidence outpaces user evidence; and recovery metadata remains
L27@P0: underprotected. These gaps motivate a research agenda for recovery-aware financial technologies.
L28@P0: 2012 ACM Subject Classification Security and privacy → Key management

L45@P1: 1 Introduction
L46@P1: In cryptoasset systems and related financial technologies, control of a cryptographic key
L47@P1: can become control of financial value: loss may remove access to funds or services, while
L48@P1: compromised recovery may transfer that control to an attacker. Key recovery is therefore part
L49@P1: of the security boundary for systems that rely on cryptographic authorization [110, 92, 8, 95].
L50@P1: Recovery must balance two goals that pull against each other. It should prevent legitimate
L51@P1: users and institutions from being permanently locked out after loss, unavailability, or
L52@P1: operational failure. At the same time, it must not create a weaker path for theft, coercion,
L53@P1: surveillance, insider abuse, or unauthorized transfer. This tension is the core reason recovery
L54@P1: remains difficult: the mechanisms that improve availability also introduce new actors, records,
L55@P1: and decisions that must be secured.
L56@P1: Existing work proposes many mechanisms, but uses incompatible vocabulary. Recovery
L57@P1: may mean restoring cryptographic material, changing account control, moving value, reissuing
L58@P1: identity credentials, repairing custody roles, or extracting forensic artifacts. Comparisons
L59@P1: can therefore obscure what is actually restored and what risks remain after recovery.
L60@P1: This paper addresses that fragmentation through a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK)
L61@P1: focused on cryptographic key recovery for cryptoasset custody and financial technologies.
L62@P1: We center the paper on financial control, while including adjacent identity, data-protection,
L63@P1: governance, and secure-hardware work when it contributes a recovery pattern that can
L64@P1: transfer to financial systems.
L65@P1: Recovery is not one operation. A useful comparison must ask what control is restored,
L66@P1: who authorizes it, what failure it handles, and what state remains afterward.
L67@P1: 1.1 Contributions
L68@P1: This Systematization of Knowledge makes the following contributions:
L69@P1: Financial-technology corpus and scope. We construct a 118-paper discovery corpus
L70@P1: on key backup, recovery, and restoration, with auditable queries, screening flow, exclusion
L71@P1: reasons, snowballing rounds, QA threshold, and manually verified LLM-assisted screening.
L72@P1: We then derive a 77-paper synthesis corpus scoped around financial technologies while
L73@P1: retaining transferable recovery patterns from identity, hardware, and data-protection
L74@P1: systems.
L75@P1: Recovery semantics for financial control. We distinguish secret-restoring recovery
L76@P1: from control-restoring recovery and show why this distinction matters for financial systems.
L77@P1: This clarifies when a system restores the same secret and when it instead restores financial
L78@P1: control through a changed control relationship.
L79@P1: A 77-system master matrix and codebook. We code every retained system using
L80@P1: a controlled vocabulary for financial context, recovery semantics, mechanism family,
L81@P1: enrollment and storage, failure events, authorization, trust placement, adversary model,
L82@P1: post-recovery state, validation evidence, deployment status, privacy, usability, postquantum relevance, and limitations. The full version provides the complete per-system
L83@P1: matrix, while the reproducibility package provides the machine-readable matrix and its
L84@P1: codebook.
L85@P1: Evaluation vocabulary, taxonomy, and construction model. We organize mechanisms by whether they restore secrets, restore control, combine both, perform forensic
L86@P1: extraction, or define requirements. We define adversary classes and recovery-specific
L87@P1-2: safety, liveness, and privacy properties, then derive a seven-stage construction model.F. J. B. Sanchez, A. K. Iannillo, and R. State 3:3
L88@P2: Production practice checks and research agenda. We check the taxonomy against
L89@P2: six production or standards-facing recovery designs and tie six findings to matrix counts
L90@P2: and examples, including sparse user-study evidence, under-specified post-recovery hygiene,
L91@P2: metadata leakage, custody boundaries, recovery economics, inheritance, and post-quantum
L92@P2: migration.
L93@P2: 1.2 SoK Framing and Novelty
L94@P2: Motivation for systematization
L95@P2: The goal is not only to summarize prior mechanisms. We define comparable recovery
L96@P2: semantics, code every retained system into the master matrix provided in the full version,
L97@P2: and separate secret reconstruction from restored financial control. A threshold wallet that
L98@P2: reconstructs an old seed, a smart account that rotates ownership, and a recovery service that
L99@P2: moves assets are all recovery systems, but they leave different post-recovery states and abuse
L100@P2: paths.
L101@P2: Novelty relative to closest related work
L102@P2: Prior work usually studies one slice of the problem: cryptocurrency protocols and DeFi,
L103@P2: wallet protocols and attacks, threshold recovery, deterministic or hardware-wallet designs,
L104@P2: smart-account recovery, identity recovery, or forensic extraction. This SoK contributes a
L105@P2: cross-domain comparison centered on recovery semantics rather than mechanism names. Its
L106@P2: novelty claims are: (i) secret-restoring and control-restoring recovery should be evaluated
L107@P2: separately; (ii) post-recovery state is a first-class security property for financial systems; and
L108@P2: (iii) recovery evidence must connect cryptographic mechanisms with operational controls,
L109@P2: metadata exposure, production practice, and human behavior. Table 1 compares the closest
L110@P2: prior-work clusters.
L111@P2: 2 Background and Scope
L112@P2: This paper uses the term cryptographic key recovery broadly, but not without distinction.
L113@P2: In the corpus, recovery may mean reconstructing an original private key, regenerating a
L114@P2: deterministic seed, restoring a key share, reissuing a credential, transferring signing authority,
L115@P2: recovering account control, or moving assets to a new control path. These operations differ
L116@P2: in what they restore and in the risks they introduce.
L117@P2: The primary scope is financial technology: systems in which cryptographic material
L118@P2: authorizes assets, transactions, account access, custody operations, or credentials used by
L119@P2: financial infrastructure. This includes blockchain wallets, smart-contract accounts, custody
L120@P2: systems, decentralized applications, decentralized identity, and secure hardware when they
L121@P2: support financial control or transferable recovery patterns.
L122@P2: The paper also considers non-financial work when it contributes a mechanism relevant to
L123@P2: financial systems. Examples include identity-management recovery, data-protection recovery,
L124@P2: governance-related recovery, and hardware-enforced recovery. These systems are included
L125@P2: because financial technologies often reuse the same primitives and operational patterns:
L126@P2: secret sharing, threshold reconstruction, deterministic derivation, secure elements, trusted
L127@P2: authorities, biometric or physical anchoring, and delegated recovery.
